content: Glutamic acid, also known as Glu or E, is one of the 20 proteinogenic amino acids. Its codons are GAA and GAG. It is classified as a non-essential amino acid, meaning the human body can synthesize it. The carboxylate anions and salts derived from glutamic acid are referred to as glutamates. In the field of neuroscience, glutamate functions as a critical neurotransmitter, playing a pivotal role in long-term potentiation, a process essential for learning and memory. At physiological pH, glutamic acid predominantly exists in its negatively charged, deprotonated carboxylate form. Although glutamic acid and other amino acids naturally occur in many foods, their flavor contributions were not scientifically identified until the early 20th century. The compound was first discovered in 1866 by German chemist Karl Heinrich Leopold Ritthausen. In 1907, Japanese researcher Kikunae Ikeda from Tokyo Imperial University identified brown crystals of glutamic acid left behind after evaporating a large volume of kombu broth. These crystals reproduced the distinct flavor he had detected in various foods, particularly seaweed. Professor Ikeda named this flavor umami and later patented a method for mass-producing monosodium glutamate (MSG), a crystalline salt of glutamic acid. Glutamate is a central molecule in cellular metabolism. In humans, dietary proteins are broken down into amino acids during digestion, which serve as metabolic fuel and perform other functional roles in the body. A key process in amino acid metabolism is transamination, where the amino group of an amino acid is transferred to an α-keto acid, typically catalyzed by a transaminase enzyme. A common α-keto acid involved in this process is α-ketoglutarate, an intermediate in the citric acid cycle. Transamination of α-ketoglutarate produces glutamate, while the resulting α-keto acid product often serves as a substrate for further metabolic processes or as a source of energy. Examples include pyruvate and oxaloacetate, which are key intermediates in glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, and the citric acid cycle. Glutamate also plays a significant role in nitrogen disposal, as it undergoes deamination via the enzyme glutamate dehydrogenase, producing ammonia, which is subsequently excreted as urea after synthesis in the liver. This linkage between transamination and deamination allows nitrogen from amino acids to be removed and excreted efficiently. In the vertebrate nervous system, glutamate is the most abundant excitatory neurotransmitter. It is stored in vesicles at chemical synapses and released in response to nerve impulses from the presynaptic cell. On the postsynaptic cell, glutamate binds to and activates receptors such as the NMDA receptor. Glutamate's role in synaptic plasticity makes it essential for cognitive functions like learning and memory. Long-term potentiation, a form of synaptic plasticity, occurs at glutamatergic synapses in brain regions such as the hippocampus and neocortex. Glutamate also facilitates synaptic crosstalk through spillover signaling, where glutamate released from one synapse influences neighboring synapses, contributing to extrasynaptic signaling or volume transmission. Glutamate transporters in neuronal and glial membranes rapidly remove glutamate from the extracellular space to maintain homeostasis. However, in cases of brain injury or disease, these transporters can operate in reverse, leading to an accumulation of extracellular glutamate. This excess glutamate can cause calcium ions to enter cells via NMDA receptor channels, resulting in neuronal damage and cell death, a phenomenon known as excitotoxicity. Mechanisms of excitotoxicity include mitochondrial damage from elevated intracellular calcium levels and the activation of pro-apoptotic gene transcription. Excitotoxicity is implicated in the ischemic cascade associated with stroke and neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Alzheimer's disease, and certain forms of mental retardation and autism. Glutamic acid has also been linked to epileptic seizures, as its microinjection into neurons induces spontaneous depolarizations resembling paroxysmal depolarizing shifts observed in epilepsy. Glutamate serves as the precursor for the synthesis of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), an inhibitory neurotransmitter, in GABAergic neurons. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), which is highly abundant in the cerebellum and pancreas. Stiff-person syndrome, a neurological disorder, is caused by anti-GAD antibodies, leading to reduced GABA synthesis and impaired motor function, such as muscle stiffness and spasms. Since GAD is also abundant in the pancreas, autoimmune destruction of pancreatic cells can occur, resulting in diabetes mellitus. Free glutamic acid is naturally present in various foods, including cheese and soy sauce, and is responsible for the umami taste, one of the five basic human taste sensations. It is commonly used as a food additive and flavor enhancer in the form of monosodium glutamate (MSG). Excellent dietary sources of glutamic acid include meats, poultry, fish, eggs, dairy products, and kombu. Some protein-rich plant foods also provide glutamic acid, with wheat protein containing 30–35% glutamic acid. Approximately 95% of dietary glutamate is metabolized by intestinal cells during the first pass. In plants, glutamic acid is utilized in growth-promoting preparations such as Auxigro, which contains 30% glutamic acid. China is the largest producer of glutamic acid globally, with the Fufeng Group Limited leading production, followed by Meihua. Together, the top five producers account for approximately 50% of the Chinese market, with an annual production capacity of 7 million tons. Pharmacologically, the drug phencyclidine (PCP) non-competitively antagonizes glutamic acid at the NMDA receptor. Similarly, sub-anesthetic doses of ketamine produce dissociative and hallucinogenic effects by targeting the same receptor. Glutamate does not easily cross the blood-brain barrier but is transported via a high-affinity transport system or converted into glutamine. Experimental techniques to detect glutamate in intact cells include the use of genetically engineered nanosensors. These nanosensors consist of a glutamate-binding protein fused to two fluorescent proteins. When glutamate binds, the fluorescence changes due to resonance between the fluorophores, enabling optical detection of glutamate concentration. Synthetic analogs of glutamic acid that can be activated by ultraviolet light and two-photon excitation microscopy have also been developed. This method of photostimulation is useful for mapping neuronal connections and understanding synapse function. In invertebrates, such as arthropods and nematodes, glutamate stimulates glutamate-gated chloride channels, which are targeted by anthelmintic drugs like avermectins. These drugs irreversibly activate the alpha subunit of the channels, causing hyperpolarization at synapses and neuromuscular junctions, leading to flaccid paralysis and death of the parasites. In the Drosophila brain, extracellular glutamate regulates postsynaptic receptor clustering through receptor desensitization. A gene expressed in glial cells actively transports glutamate into the extracellular space, while in the nucleus accumbens, stimulation of group II metabotropic glutamate receptors reduces extracellular glutamate levels. This suggests that extracellular glutamate may play an endocrine-like role in a larger homeostatic system.
